subject: best way to build models in occuRN

messages.author: 83210b42d6e7063d
messages.subject: best way to build models in occuRN
parts:
Hello,

I am using occuRN to model the abundance of dogs at two locations. I have two site covariates, camera (4 levels) and habitat (3 levels), and one observation covariate, time since lure deployment (recorded on 10 occasions). I can run and interpret models, but am after some advice on how best to build my models and why? Should I be building my models based on logic? For example, it does not make sense for camera to influence abundance and so i should not include it as a covariate on abundance. Or, should I be investigating all possible model combinations? If this is the case, should I also be investigating interactions, even though they would not be expected or logical? I have seen both methods of model building used in statistical modelling before.

Thanks for the advice,

Shaun

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: best way to build models in occuRN
parts:
Hi Shaun,

At the very least, I think that there would probably be universal agreement that you should *not* use camera as a covariate for lambda--there are things that might effect both state and observation processes (perhaps habitat, for example), but changing a camera model does not seem like it should effect abundance. The degree to which users fit all possible combinations vs. a predefined set of models varies in practice (recent literature should suggest what people using RN/occupancy/capture-recapture/Nmix models
are generally doing), but in all cases, there is at least some(?) threshold of logic being used to define which models are fit. 

As far as the 'right' way to generate a set of models/perform model selection or the appropriate stringency of any logical threshold that should be employed...ehhh...maybe your best bet is to take a look at the large body of literature on that topic (in ecology in particular). Not that there's some secret knowledge out there that can't be publicly disclosed (or maybe there is, but I don't know about it), but the philosophy of scientific inquiry is a pretty broad topic.

--John

messages.author: dc8b4131b39a099f
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: best way to build models in occuRN
parts:
Hi Shaun. I agree w John, regarding "camera" as a covariate on lambda: if it doesn't make sense as a biological hypothesis representing reality on the ground, then it shouldn't be a competing model, and likewise for any covariates. I'm not aware of any rule or justification always necessitating a fully "nested" model set containing all possible combinations of covariates. In my opinion, model sets should represent competing hypotheses developed to answer specific questions and be given thorough consideration before any models are fit (ie, "a priori" models). Regarding interactions, I'm under the impression that they are sometimes or often avoided because some find them more difficult to program and interpret, but I often find them to be the most informative components of a model. I'd wager a bet that interactions are present far more often than not in biological systems and data.

I found David Anderson's Model-based Inferences in the Life Sciences really useful as a grad student, as far as understanding both the quantitative and conceptual basis for building sets of competing models that most effectively answer the questions posed. It's a bit less technical than Burnham and Anderson's Model Selection and Multimodel Inference. Like John said, the wealth of literature on model inference is extensive. Happy hunting.

Matt
